paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Κριτόβουλος τῷ Σωκράτει διαλέγεται περὶ χρημάτων. πολλὰ μὲν ἔχει, πλείω δὲ ζητεῖ. ὁ Σωκράτης ὀλίγα ἔχει· ὅμως δὲ οὐ πλείω ζητεῖ.
Ὁ Σωκράτης λέγει· «ἐμοὶ τὰ ἐμὰ ἱκανά ἐστιν· σοὶ δὲ τὰ σὰ οὐχ ἱκανά.» ὁ Κριτόβουλος γελᾷ. πλουσιώτερος γὰρ εἶναι δοκεῖ τοῦ Σωκράτους.
Ὁ μὲν Κριτόβουλος μείζονα οἰκίαν καὶ πλείονα χρήματα ἔχει. ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης ἐλάττονα ζητεῖ. οὐ γὰρ ἡ αὐτὴ χρεία ἀμφοτέροις ἐστίν.
Ὁ Κριτόβουλος ξένους δέχεται καὶ τοὺς πολίτας θεραπεύει. ἡ πόλις δὲ χρήματα αἰτεῖ. οὐ μόνον τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἔργα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ κοινὰ σκοπεῖ.
Τί οὖν ἄμεινόν ἐστιν; πλείω ἔχειν ἢ ἐλαττόνων δεῖσθαι; ὁ μὲν πλουσιώτατος οὐ πάντοτε εὐδαιμονέστατός ἐστιν. πολλάκις γὰρ οὐχ ἡσυχώτερον ζῇ.
Ὁ Σωκράτης οὐ τῶν πενήτων καταφρονεῖ. τὴν χρείαν πρὸς τὰ χρήματα συγκρίνει. ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τὸ «πλέον» οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστι τῷ «ἱκανόν».

reading.translation:
Critobulus talks with Socrates about money. He has much, but seeks more. Socrates has little; nevertheless he does not seek more.

Socrates says, “My possessions are sufficient for me, but yours are not sufficient for you.” Critobulus laughs. For he seems to be richer than Socrates.

Critobulus has a larger house and more money. Socrates seeks less. For both men do not have the same need.

Critobulus receives guests and attends to his fellow citizens. The city asks for money. He considers not only his own affairs but also public affairs.

What, then, is better: to have more or to need less? The richest person is not always the happiest. For he often does not live more peacefully.

Socrates does not look down on poor people. He compares need with resources. In the argument, “more” is not the same as “enough.”

blocks.title: οἶκος and οἰκονομία
body: οἶκος can mean a house or the household and resources associated with it. οἰκονομία concerns managing that sphere. The English word “economy” should not make us assume the ancient dialogue uses all our modern categories.
χρήματα often means resources, property, or money. Context decides how narrow the sense should be. A comparison about χρήματα is not necessarily a comparison of coins in a purse.

sections.title: 1. Regular comparatives and superlatives
body: A comparative sets one item against another; a superlative places it at an extreme within a group. Many adjectives use -τερος and -τατος: σοφός, σοφώτερος, σοφώτατος. Vowel length in the stem affects the connecting vowel; learn the listed forms.

Comparatives and superlatives still agree with their nouns. The ending -τερος does not remove gender, number, or case. A superlative can also have an intensive sense, “very wise,” where no definite comparison group is stated.

sections.title: 2. Irregular comparison
body: Frequent adjectives may change stems. ἀγαθός has βελτίων/βέλτιστος for “better/best”; κακός has χείρων/χείριστος; πολύς has πλείων/πλεῖστος; ὀλίγος has ἐλάττων/ἐλάχιστος. Meaning and context govern the choice among alternative Greek forms.

Comparatives in -ων have masculine/feminine nominative singular -ων and neuter -ον. βελτίονα and βελτίω are alternative accusative singular masculine/feminine forms. Recognize these contracted alternatives without treating them as different degrees.

sections.title: 3. Than: genitive or ἤ
body: Greek can express the second term of comparison with a genitive: σοφώτερος τοῦ φίλου, “wiser than the friend.” Alternatively ἤ introduces the comparison, and the case follows the parallel construction: οὗτος σοφώτερός ἐστιν ἢ ἐκεῖνος.

A superlative often takes a partitive genitive: σοφώτατος τῶν φίλων, “wisest of the friends.” Distinguish this group from the genitive used after a comparative. Do not confuse either with a possessive genitive.

checks.prompt: What does τῶν φίλων supply after σοφώτατος?
checks.answer: the group within which he is wisest

sections.title: 4. Comparing actions and needs
body: An adverb modifies an action or description rather than agreeing with a noun. Comparative adverbs commonly use the neuter singular comparative adjective; superlative adverbs use the neuter plural superlative: σοφώτερον, σοφώτατα.

In the reading, more possessions do not automatically produce better living. Keep the grammar precise: βέλτιον ζῆν compares ways of living; βελτίων βίος describes a life. μᾶλλον and μάλιστα are useful general adverbs meaning “more” and “most.”

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Oeconomicus
body: The Oeconomicus explores the management of an oikos: household, property, work, and people. Its title gives us a distant ancestor of “economics,” but its subject is not identical to a modern national economy. Socrates talks first with Critobulus; later he recounts a conversation with Ischomachus.

The dialogue’s twenty-one chapters move from the meaning of wealth to the organization of an estate. Socrates first questions Critobulus about whether possessions actually benefit their owner. He then recounts an extended conversation with Ischomachus, a prosperous gentleman-farmer, about marriage, household organization, agriculture, and directing other people’s work. The shift lets a philosophical question become a tour of everyday decisions.

Read with two questions in mind: what makes management effective, and whose interests define success? Ischomachus describes his young wife’s education and the work of enslaved people from the position of a male household head. His account gives access to ideals of cooperation and order while also revealing unequal authority. Socrates’ questions invite scrutiny; a speaker’s confidence is not a reason to accept every assumption.

Reading invitation: compare chapter 1 on useful possessions with chapters 8–9 on order, then look at chapter 21 on leadership. Could a person have excellent equipment yet manage badly? The English edition linked below calls the work The Economist. Its subject is the oikos—household, estate, and people—rather than economics in the modern national sense.

Our selection comes from chapter 2. Socrates provocatively compares his own small resources with Critobulus’s much greater resources and obligations. The dialogue asks whether wealth is measured by an inventory alone or by what a person needs to accomplish.

sections.title: An estate is not a bank balance
body: A household’s resources could include land, equipment, stored produce, and the labor of people with unequal status. Counting possessions leaves out maintenance, obligations, and who controls the work.

The lesson’s resource comparison is deliberately qualitative. We have not converted an ancient estate into a modern salary or assigned an invented market price to the banner’s objects. The point is the relationship between means and demands.

sections.title: The surprise of the comparison
body: Socrates’s challenge works because Critobulus seems obviously wealthier. A comparative such as πλουσιώτερος can describe possessions, while a different comparison asks who has enough. Those claims need not have the same answer.

Try a two-column inventory for an imaginary journey: resources on one side, necessary demands on the other. Add one obligation that makes the apparently richer traveler less secure. This is a reasoning exercise, not advice that poverty is good.

sections.title: Whose “enough” counts?
body: The household manager’s comfort is not the only perspective. Ask whether the people doing the work have enough rest, food, and security. Xenophon’s household discussion is shaped by ancient inequalities; we can read closely while asking questions its speakers do not fully answer.
Use one comparative, one superlative, and one comparative adverb to explain your judgment: a larger store, the most urgent need, acting more wisely. Keep the three constructions distinct.
